newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Bank of Ireland boosted by strong economy.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Ireland boosted by strong economy.

text.p: Bank of Ireland Plc, one of the Republic of Ireland's largest financial groups, on Wednesday announced higher annual profits and dividends and said the strong economy should steer it towards more growth this year.

"The outlook and conditions in all the markets in which we are operating are good...here, the United States, everywhere. Pressure on margins continues but we will continue to see good performance and good volume growth," chief executive Pat Molloy said in a telephone interview.

The bank, Ireland's oldest, raised pretax profits in the year to end-March 1997 by 8.8 percent to 395.6 million Irish pounds ($600.5 million). It proposed a final dividend of 11.65 pence, bringing the total payout to 17.75p after 15.25p a year earlier.

The figures were broadly in line with analysts' expectations and Bank of Ireland shares showed little reaction, easing 4p in London to 690-1/2p in modest volume and trading unchanged at 744 Irish pence in Dublin.
"We haven't produced any surprises. The Irish economy continues to perform very well and the outlook is good. It's a good time to be in the banking business," Molloy said.

Bank of Ireland said it raised its income by almost eight percent to 923.3 million Irish pounds while cost growth was held at 4.4 percent, cutting the group cost/income ratio by two percentage points to 59 percent. Net interest income rose 5.6 percent to 608.1 million pounds.

Despite the 8.8 percent gain in annual profit, earnings per share grew only marginally, rising to 52.0p from 51.6p because the group was now fully liable for tax on its share of profits from the U.S. Citizens Financial Group.

The bank raised pre-tax profit at its retail division by 11.8 percent to 204.4 million Irish pounds as the strong economy pushed lending up 12 percent. Profits rose in the Republic of Ireland, Britain and Northern Ireland. The bank said it continued to perform well in the domestic mortgage market, taking 20 percent of new Irish mortgages.
Molloy said his bank's strong performance, with assets totalling 19.7 billion Irish pounds, meant provisions remained modest at 20 million pounds, down slightly from the previous year.
The bank said profits at its corporate and treasury division were satisfactory despite a lower rate of loan loss recoveries. Pretax profit slipped 1.4 percent to 73.9 million Irish pounds.

Molloy defended his bank's record on dividends, which analysts have described as cautious with cover almost as high as three times earnings. The bank last year bought Britain's Bristol & West, one of the country's top 10 building societies, for 600 million sterling cash and analysts expected the bank to focus on rebuilding capital.

"We had a large flood of capital (to pay for Bristol & West) but we believe in a progressive dividend policy. We think cover of three times is a bit too strong but we are producing a pretty good dividend increase of 16 percent," he said.
